examples.whatToDo: When giving a forecast that multiple people will act on differently, state a specific probability. The number makes your belief available to the room at a single value rather than at whatever value each listener brings to it.
examples.whyItMatters: Verbal probability language distributes interpretation. A room of ten listeners walks away with ten different numbers from the same word. When those listeners make different decisions, they are not disagreeing with each other; they are responding to different beliefs they projected onto your forecast. A number forces a shared starting point.

examples.title: Diego fills in the blank column and finds the number contradicts three weeks of meetings

planSpec.domain: venture capital firm where a partner asks an analyst to put a probability on a portfolio company's Series B milestone
planSpec.audience: an analyst who has been saying 'I think it looks good' for three weeks and is now asked for a number
planSpec.stakes: a pro-rata investment decision worth $800K
planSpec.requiredBeat: when forced to write a specific percentage, the analyst realizes she has been shading her verbal confidence upward to avoid seeming negative; the number forces her to confront what she actually believes

examples.scenario:
'Just put a number in the column,' the partner says, sliding the deal memo across the table. 'Don't overthink it.'

Diego opens his laptop. He has been saying 'looking good' and 'I think they'll get there' in every check-in for three weeks. He types 65%, looks at it, deletes it, types 68%, deletes that, goes back to 65%.

The number feels different from the words. The words were directional and vague; they conveyed enthusiasm without specifying what he actually thought the odds were. 65% is specific enough that he can feel the gap between it and the upbeat tone he has been projecting. He had been shading his verbal confidence upward to avoid seeming negative about a deal the firm was interested in. The 65% is what he actually believed. It does not match how he has been talking.

The partner reads the number and nods. 'So we're basically coin-flipping plus a bit.' Diego says yes. They spend the next thirty minutes discussing what would move the estimate in either direction, something they had not done in any of the three weeks of 'looking good' check-ins. Diego must decide by end of week whether to recommend the pro-rata investment on the current terms or push for a milestone condition before the firm commits the $800K.
examples.whatToDo: When a significant decision depends on a forward-looking assessment, write a specific probability before the meeting rather than arriving with verbal language. The act of producing the number surfaces what you actually believe rather than what you want the room to hear.
examples.whyItMatters: Verbal confidence language is easy to shade upward or downward depending on the social context. A specific number is harder to shade without noticing. Diego's 65% could not be presented as enthusiastic optimism; it required a different conversation. That conversation was the one the $800K decision needed.

examples.title: Camille replaces 'guarded prognosis' with 38% and finds the family had heard something much worse

planSpec.domain: oncology team giving a prognosis to a family
planSpec.audience: an oncologist who has been using 'guarded prognosis' and 'challenging case' with a family hearing those words as near-certain bad news
planSpec.stakes: the family's treatment decisions, which hinge on whether they understand 5-year survival as 20%, 40%, or lower
planSpec.requiredBeat: the oncologist switches to a number and the family's response shifts; they had been hearing the verbal hedges as single digits, and the 38% opens a different conversation about treatment intensity

examples.scenario:
Three weeks of family consultations in the family conference room, and Camille has been using the same language: guarded prognosis, challenging case, difficult road ahead. Medically accurate. Empathetic in register. She has not said a number because numbers feel stark.

In the fourth consultation, she asks how the family is processing things. The daughter says they have already begun talking to a hospice coordinator. Their private assumption has been 5-10% survival. Camille had been thinking 38% at comparable stage and age.

She recalibrates the conversation. Thirty-eight percent five-year survival at this stage and this patient's profile. The room changes. Thirty-eight is not hope in any simple sense, but it is not single digits either. It opens a different set of questions: what does treatment intensity look like at this probability? What does the family want to preserve? What would a partial response mean for quality of life?

The conversations that followed that session were more specific and more useful than the three weeks of guarded language that preceded them. Camille had not changed what she believed. She had changed what the family could work with. She must decide what treatment intensity to recommend: whether to pursue aggressive therapy, which the 38% survival figure may support, or a more conservative approach the family might prefer given their earlier assumptions.
examples.whatToDo: When families or patients are making significant decisions based on a prognosis, name a specific survival or outcome probability rather than a verbal characterization. The number allows a shared starting point for the decisions that follow.
examples.whyItMatters: Verbal probability language in clinical settings carries enormous interpretive variance. 'Guarded prognosis' can mean anything from 5% to 50% depending on what the listener brings to it. The gap between the clinician's intended meaning and the family's heard meaning can produce decisions nobody would endorse once the gap is visible.

examples.title: Three weeks of 'on track' ends when the question becomes a percentage

planSpec.domain: software project delivery where an engineering lead is asked for a ship probability before a stakeholder review
planSpec.audience: a lead engineer who has been saying 'we're on track' at every standup for three weeks
planSpec.stakes: a quarterly board presentation where the product announcement has already been scripted
planSpec.requiredBeat: when asked for an actual percentage, the lead says 55% — a number that contradicts the 'on track' signal and forces a conversation that the verbal hedges had been suppressing for three weeks

examples.scenario:
You are an engineering lead who has typed 'looking good for Q3' in the standup thread four days running. The product VP asks to meet before the board presentation and says she needs an actual percentage on delivery confidence.

You say 55%.

The VP stares at the number for a moment. She had been planning a product announcement around this delivery for six weeks. 'On track' had been her signal that 55% was not the right number to plan around.

You explain: the core feature is solid, but two dependencies are owned by another team that has been running late on a separate initiative. You had not surfaced this explicitly because 'on track' is what you say when the train has not stopped yet. 55% is what you believe when you actually ask yourself whether the train will arrive.

The next hour is the most productive planning conversation of the quarter. The VP adjusts the board presentation from an announcement to a preview. Two engineers get redirected to unblock the dependencies. The conversation that 55% opened was not available to 'on track.' You must now decide whether to keep issuing percentage estimates in future standups, even knowing some team members will find them unsettling, or return to status language once this delivery risk is resolved.
examples.whatToDo: Before any stakeholder meeting where a project status will inform a downstream decision, write a specific probability on delivery or completion. Translate your internal confidence into a number the decision-maker can act on rather than a phrase they will interpret through their own optimism.
examples.whyItMatters: 'On track' is a status, not an estimate. It tells the listener the current state without committing to the probability of the future state. The gap between 'on track' and 55% is not a failure of honesty; it is a structural property of status language. A probability forces the honest commitment that status language allows you to defer.

examples.title: Maja writes 70% and finds her own brief argues for three different numbers at once

planSpec.domain: legislative policy analyst at a think tank asked to estimate the probability of a state bill passing
planSpec.audience: a senior analyst whose written brief uses 'strong likelihood' throughout
planSpec.stakes: a nonprofit deciding whether to build a pilot program contingent on the bill passing
planSpec.requiredBeat: the analyst writes 70%, reads her brief again, and realizes three paragraphs imply 90%+ confidence while one caveat implies closer to 50%; the number exposes an inconsistency the verbal language had been hiding

examples.scenario:
The grant committee packet is sitting on the table, her brief printed and stapled inside it. Someone has written 'what does strong likelihood mean here?' in pencil in the margin of page three and put a question mark after it.

Maja has written the phrase 'strong likelihood of passage' six times in nine pages. She knows what she means by it. The question is whether the committee knows.

She writes 70% on a notepad. Then she reads her brief again with the 70% in mind. The opening section implies the bill is nearly certain; the coalition analysis in section two implies passage above 90% given the vote count she projects. The risk paragraph near the end, the one she added because she knew the analysis was not airtight, implies something closer to 50% if the floor schedule slips.

Seventy percent cannot coexist comfortably with any of those three readings. The number has revealed that 'strong likelihood' had been doing different work in different parts of the brief. She revises the brief to make the logic consistent with 70%, which means changing two claims in section two and expanding the risk paragraph into a clear statement of the conditions that would shift the estimate downward.

The grant committee funds the pilot. The brief's estimate of 70% is specific enough that when the bill passes the committee vote six weeks later, the nonprofit knows to treat the revised vote-count as the next checkpoint.
examples.whatToDo: Before submitting any analysis that uses verbal probability language, translate your overall probability into a number, then read your document with that number visible. Where the document is inconsistent with the number, revise the document.
examples.whyItMatters: Verbal hedges like 'strong likelihood' can hold contradictory beliefs in the same document without flagging the contradiction. A number forces a single commitment that makes internal inconsistency visible. The revision process is part of the forecast quality, not just the communication of it.

examples.title: Etienne writes split-time numbers and discovers two athletes he was confident about have no evidence behind that confidence

planSpec.domain: competitive rowing coach tracking athlete split-time improvement predictions before a major regatta
planSpec.audience: a coach who has been describing expected improvements with verbal phrases like 'you should be stronger by the time we get there'
planSpec.stakes: athlete training intensity decisions for the final six weeks before the regatta
planSpec.requiredBeat: the switch from verbal to numerical predictions forces the coach to notice that two athletes he has been verbally confident about have insufficient training data to support better than 50% confidence; the numbers expose the gap between his confidence as a coach and the evidence behind it

examples.scenario:
At 6:00 a.m. on a Monday in October, Etienne opens his training log and begins filling in a new column: predicted split-time improvement per 500m before the November regatta. He has twelve athletes and six weeks.

For eight of them, he writes numbers without trouble: 1.4 seconds, 0.9 seconds, 1.2 seconds. The training data is consistent and the improvement curves are clear. For two athletes in the middle of the roster, he pauses. He has been telling them 'you're going to be strong by November' in practice. He means it. He believes in them as athletes.

But when he tries to write a number, he cannot write one that feels grounded. Both athletes have had inconsistent attendance over the six weeks of available data. One had an injury in week three that disrupted the progression. He writes 0.6 seconds for one and 0.5 seconds for the other, then adds a note to himself: less than 50% confidence in these estimates.

The six weeks that follow are different for those two athletes. He redirects training focus to address the inconsistency in their data rather than assuming the improvement will materialize from belief alone. One of them hits 0.7 seconds at the regatta. The other misses the target but improves enough that the training adjustment was clearly right. The log now has predicted values and actual values for every rower.
examples.whatToDo: Before any performance review or projection, write down a specific number for what you expect and note your confidence level in that number separately. The confidence level is the diagnostic: when it is low, the number is telling you something about the evidence, not just the outcome.
examples.whyItMatters: Verbal encouragement and a probability estimate are different claims. 'You will be strong by November' is motivational. '0.6 seconds, less than 50% confidence' is an assessment. A coach who conflates the two is running two jobs with one sentence, and neither is done well. The number separates the belief from the evidence behind the belief.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of using a numerical probability instead of a verbal hedge like 'likely' or 'strong likelihood'?
choices: To signal quantitative rigor and analytical expertise to the reader, improving perceived credibility.
To reduce the time that audiences need to interpret and act on a forecast in a shared setting.
To produce a claim specific enough that its accuracy can be checked after the outcome arrives.
questions.explanation: The core purpose is accountability. A verbal hedge like 'likely' can be reinterpreted after the fact to fit whatever the outcome was. A numerical probability produces a claim that either holds or does not when the outcome arrives, making the forecaster's accuracy visible over time. Signaling expertise and reducing interpretation time are secondary benefits, not the mechanism.

questions.prompt: An analyst consistently uses 'high confidence' in policy briefs. A review of 40 such briefs finds she was right on 60% of the occasions when she used that phrase. What does this reveal about her calibration?
choices: Her stated confidence is poorly calibrated: 'high confidence' is tracking near 60% accuracy when it should reflect accuracy near 80-90%.
She is performing adequately at 60%, given the well-documented inherent difficulty of policy forecasting in uncertain domains.
40 briefs is a sample too small to draw reliable conclusions about calibration from verbal probability language alone.
questions.explanation: If 'high confidence' in standard usage implies accuracy well above 60%, then a 60% hit rate on those claims is a calibration problem, not adequate performance. Calibration means stated confidence matches actual accuracy. A 60% hit rate on high-confidence claims signals that her stated certainty level is consistently exceeding what her accuracy earns. The sample of 40 is small but sufficient for a working calibration estimate.

questions.prompt: A project manager says 'we'll probably hit the Q3 milestone' at a stakeholder meeting. Applying Sherman Kent's argument about verbal probability language, what should she do instead?
choices: Use more specific verbal language such as 'very high probability' or 'nearly certain.'
State a specific percentage she actually believes and a condition she would check when Q3 arrives.
Provide a detailed explanation of the obstacles so stakeholders can form their own probability estimate.
questions.explanation: Kent's argument was that verbal hedges allow different readers to extract different numbers from the same phrase, preventing accountability later. A specific percentage leaves no room for reinterpretation and commits the forecaster to a claim that can be scored when Q3 arrives. More specific verbal language does not solve the problem; it just relocates the ambiguity. Detailed obstacle-sharing transfers interpretation to listeners rather than resolving it.

questions.prompt: Why is 'strong likelihood' more costly as a forecasting claim than '70% probability,' even when both represent the same underlying belief?
choices: Because 'strong likelihood' can be interpreted as anywhere from 50% to 95% by different readers, making cross-reader coordination and later accountability impossible.
Because verbal probability language lacks the mathematical precision and specificity required for sound institutional decision-making and post-outcome review.
Because a stated percentage like '70%' conveys stronger expert credibility and analytical authority than verbal hedges in most professional settings.
questions.explanation: The problem is not mathematical precision for its own sake; it is interpretive drift. Different readers extract different numbers from 'strong likelihood,' so the same phrase produces different decisions in different parts of an organization. After the outcome, both a reader who heard 90% and one who heard 55% can claim their interpretation matched the analyst's intent. The numerical claim prevents this by locking in a single interpretation that can be checked.

questions.prompt: A scientist reports 'elevated risk' of an extreme weather event without specifying a probability. One agency treats it as near-certain; another treats it as routine. What failure does this illustrate?
choices: The scientist communicated irresponsibly by defaulting to specialist technical language when addressing a broad public policy audience.
Decision-makers in both agencies lack sufficient training to interpret probabilistic claims from scientists without explicit numerical guidance.
Verbal probability language gives different readers license to assign different numbers to the same phrase, producing different decisions from the same assessment.
questions.explanation: The failure is structural, not a training problem or a communication style error. When a probability claim is verbal rather than numerical, each reader assigns their own number to it. The scientist's intent becomes irrelevant; the phrase becomes a mirror for pre-existing beliefs. A numerical claim eliminates this by producing a single interpretable estimate that both agencies must respond to.

questions.prompt: An oncologist tells a family their loved one faces a 'guarded prognosis.' The family makes treatment decisions based on what they heard. The oncologist later says she meant 35-40% five-year survival. What error occurred?
choices: The family should have asked clarifying questions before making irreversible treatment decisions.
The verbal phrase allowed a large misread that shaped major decisions, because it carried no single interpretable probability.
The oncologist's 35-40% range was itself too imprecise to communicate reliably.
questions.explanation: The gap between the physician's intended 35-40% and the family's heard interpretation was not a failure of listening; it is a structural property of verbal probability language. 'Guarded prognosis' carries no number, so the family supplied their own. A stated numerical probability would have produced a shared starting point. Asking families to seek clarification places the burden on people least equipped to know what question to ask.

questions.prompt: Why does writing a specific probability number change the forecaster's own thinking before it changes the audience's understanding?
choices: Because producing a specific number requires the forecaster to commit to a value rather than defaulting to language elastic enough to contain multiple beliefs simultaneously.
Because numerical estimates take longer to produce, giving the forecaster more time to consider the evidence.
Because forecasters experience social accountability when colleagues see a specific number that verbal phrases do not trigger.
questions.explanation: A verbal hedge like 'likely' can be produced without knowing what you actually think; it fits inside a wide range of beliefs at once. Writing 65% requires you to rule out 60% and 70% and commit to a specific value. That commitment forces a confrontation with uncertainty that the verbal hedge allows you to skip entirely. The preparation time and social effects are real but secondary to this primary cognitive mechanism.

questions.prompt: An analyst writes 70% in a brief where three paragraphs imply 90%+ confidence and one caveat implies closer to 50%. The number cannot be reconciled with either. What has the exercise of writing the number achieved?
choices: It revealed that the analyst's evidence base is too thin to support any probability estimate.
It produced a number that represents the mathematical average of her various internal confidence levels.
It made an internal inconsistency visible that verbal hedges had been holding in place without revealing.
questions.explanation: The inconsistency was present before the number was written. Verbal language ('strong likelihood') is elastic enough to hold contradictory beliefs simultaneously without flagging the contradiction. Writing the number forced a single commitment that could not coexist with both the optimistic paragraphs and the cautious caveat. The number did not average her beliefs; it made the incoherence between them visible and required resolution.

questions.prompt: A manager argues that numerical probabilities suggest false certainty in inherently unpredictable domains, and that verbal hedges more honestly reflect the limits of knowledge. Is this argument valid?
choices: Yes, because numerical probability claims are only appropriate in domains where there are sufficient historical base rates and stable feedback cycles for meaningful calibration.

Partly, because the concern about false certainty applies to poorly calibrated numbers, not to numerical probability as a practice; a well-stated range can communicate uncertainty more precisely than a verbal hedge.
No, because verbal hedges never truly communicate genuine uncertainty to listeners; they always conceal or distort the forecaster's actual underlying beliefs.
questions.explanation: A numerical range like '35-65%' communicates the scope of uncertainty more precisely than 'could go either way.' The false certainty concern applies to overconfident point estimates, not to the practice of quantification itself. The manager's objection assumes verbal hedges communicate uncertainty more honestly, but phrases like 'probably' mask a wide range of beliefs that a number would force into the open. Numbers can be wide or narrow; the dishonesty is in calibration, not in the practice.

reviewCards.front: What is the difference between calibration and resolution in forecasting?
reviewCards.back: Calibration is whether your stated confidence level matches your actual accuracy rate over time: a forecaster who says 70% should be right on about 70% of those predictions. Resolution is whether your predictions vary appropriately across different questions, distinguishing the 80% cases from the 40% cases rather than saying 60% on everything.

reviewCards.front: What did Sherman Kent argue about verbal probability language in intelligence assessments?
reviewCards.back: Kent argued that verbal hedges like 'probable' or 'serious possibility' allow different readers to extract different numbers from the same phrase, preventing coordinated response and making assessments impossible to audit after the fact. He pushed for numerical probability ranges to produce a single interpretable claim that could be checked when events occurred.

reviewCards.front: Why does writing a specific probability number change the forecaster's own thinking?
reviewCards.back: A verbal hedge can hold multiple beliefs simultaneously without forcing a commitment. A specific number requires ruling out nearby values and committing to a single estimate. That commitment forces the forecaster to confront their actual uncertainty level rather than defaulting to language elastic enough to mean whatever the outcome requires.

reviewCards.front: What does the Brier score measure, and why does it matter?
reviewCards.back: The Brier score measures the mean squared error between a forecaster's stated probability and the actual outcome, with zero as perfect and 0.5 as chance-level. It matters because it makes forecast quality comparable across forecasters in a single number, distinguishing a forecaster who says 70% and is right 70% of the time from one who says 90% and is right 70% of the time.

reviewCards.front: How do you test whether your numerical forecast is specific enough to be held accountable?
reviewCards.back: Ask: could you reinterpret this number after the outcome arrives without changing it? If yes, the number is not specific enough. A probability claim that can be reconciled with both the occurrence and non-occurrence of the event is functionally equivalent to a verbal hedge. Narrow the range until only one outcome would confirm it.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Replace verbal probability language with a specific number before any forecast leaves your hands. The number should be specific enough that you could not comfortably reinterpret it after the fact if the outcome differs from what you expected.

ifThenPlans.context: Before sending any written assessment, report, or brief that includes verbal probability language
ifThenPlans.plan: If a phrase like 'likely,' 'probably,' 'strong chance,' or 'good probability' appears in the document, then write the specific percentage you actually mean next to it. Read the document with that number visible. Where the document is inconsistent with the number, revise the document.

ifThenPlans.context: Before any meeting where a status update or forward-looking estimate will be shared
ifThenPlans.plan: If you plan to say 'on track,' 'looks good,' or 'I think we'll get there,' then write a specific probability before the meeting and bring that number into the room rather than the verbal phrase.

ifThenPlans.context: When you receive a forecast or assessment that uses verbal probability language
ifThenPlans.plan: If the assessment uses 'likely,' 'high confidence,' or similar phrases, then ask the person what specific percentage they mean. If they cannot name one, treat the forecast as unverifiable and weight it accordingly.

ifThenPlans.context: After an outcome arrives that you predicted verbally
ifThenPlans.plan: If you used verbal probability language rather than a specific number, then ask yourself: what percentage would I have written if I had been forced to? Compare that to the outcome. The gap between the number you would have written and how you actually communicated is where your calibration work begins.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Find one verbal hedge you used today: likely, probably, good chance, I think. Write the specific percentage you actually meant. Then write the date when the outcome of this prediction will be knowable. Keep both numbers somewhere you will find them when that date arrives.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, score one past prediction where you stated a specific probability. Note whether your stated number was consistent with the outcome in the right direction and at the right frequency. Over several months, a pattern of whether your 70% calls are actually right 70% of the time will become visible.

memorableLines.text: The verbal hedge survives because it can mean anything. The number survives only if it is right.
memorableLines.why: It collapses the entire accountability argument into two sentences: one on why verbal language persists, one on what forces the alternative to be honest.

memorableLines.text: A number does not just communicate. It diagnoses.
memorableLines.why: Six words that capture the psychological mechanism: the number reveals what the forecaster believes rather than just transmitting it.

memorableLines.text: The forecaster who builds a record gets better at forecasting. Everyone else just gets older at it.
memorableLines.why: It names the asymmetry between learning and experience: experience without feedback just accumulates time, not skill.

chapters.title: Superforecasters
chapters.hook: Staying on the hard question takes deliberate effort. The easier proxy arrives faster, generates the same feeling of analytical work, and produces an answer, which is exactly why it so often replaces the question you actually needed to answer.
chapters.counterintuition: Question substitution does not feel like taking a shortcut. The proxy question is genuinely difficult and the work feels real. The tell is that you have a confident answer ready and it covers the easier question, not the harder one you were supposed to answer.
chapters.tryThisNow: Name one decision you are currently tracking: a project timeline, a negotiation outcome, a business forecast. Write down the exact question you are trying to answer, then write down the question you have actually been spending most time on. If they are different, you have already substituted. Rewrite your most recent estimate as an answer to the original question.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Name the target question before any analysis, then check whether your conclusion addresses it or a simpler substitute. The error is invisible until you commit an answer.

breakdown.fastRead:
David circled the three liver enzyme datapoints and wrote 'pattern consistent with class effect' in the review notes. He had spent forty minutes on the analysis. The pattern did look familiar from other compounds in the same drug class. He had a confident preliminary read before the committee met.

What David had not noticed was that he had been answering a different question than the one on the review form. The form asked: what is the causal mechanism linking this compound to these enzyme elevations? The question David had been answering was: does this pattern look like something I have seen before in this class? The first question requires mechanistic evidence that had not been gathered. The second question only requires a pattern match, and pattern matches are fast.

The substituted question is not the wrong question. It is the question that arrived first, felt like the right one, and got answered while the right one waited.

The failure here is not that David worked carelessly. It is that he worked carefully on something that was not quite the task. Careful work on the wrong question produces a confident answer to the wrong question.
breakdown.deepRead:
The Iraq WMD intelligence failure is a study in substitution at scale. The question intelligence analysts needed to answer was: does Saddam Hussein actually have weapons of mass destruction? The question that actually got answered was: does his behavior resemble someone who is concealing weapons of mass destruction?

The first question requires direct evidence of the weapons' existence. The second question requires behavioral evidence, and that evidence was abundant and consistent. Hussein had expelled inspectors. He had stonewalled. His behavior was entirely consistent with concealment. And behavior consistent with concealment is the natural output of both a leader who has weapons and a leader who cannot afford to appear weak by admitting he does not.

The substitution was not stupid. Robert Jervis analyzed the case and noted the underlying judgment was understandable: the signals were genuinely ambiguous and the pattern-matching felt like rigorous analysis. What would have changed things was not a different conclusion but a different confidence level. The question on paper was whether he had the weapons. The question that actually got answered was whether he was acting like someone who did.

Expressing 70% instead of 95% would have been honest, and honesty at that confidence level moves policy. The analysts were not negligent. They answered the wrong question with full conviction.

Question substitution is invisible from the inside because the proxy question is genuinely difficult. David's pattern-matching across drug classes required expertise and judgment. The work feels like the real work. The only diagnostic is whether the target question would accept the answer being generated. If the answer only fits the proxy, the substitution has already happened.
breakdown.fullRead:
Kasia's debrief room had personality descriptors on the whiteboard. 'Collaborative.' 'Strategic thinker.' 'Strong communicator.' When one panel member said the candidate reminded her of Damien, their best VP of Engineering, no one pushed back. Kasia watched the room and noticed something: the committee was answering 'does this person resemble our best people?' instead of 'what does her measurable outcome record show for the specific skills this role requires?'

The proxy question was not dishonest. Resemblance to a top performer is a legitimate signal. The problem is that it answers an easier question ('do I recognize quality in this person?') rather than the harder one ('what evidence tells me this person will perform at this level in this role?'). The second question requires outcome data the committee was not collecting.

The question you cannot answer easily tells you something important: that you are probably not answering it.

Hugo's insurance investigation had been running for six weeks before he wrote both questions down. The question on the case file was: is this a fraudulent claim? The question he had been asking himself was: does this claimant seem like the type who files fraudulent claims? When he looked at the base rate for this claim type, he found a 3% fraud rate. His impression-based referral rate had been running at 18%. The proxy had been generating six times more referrals than the base rate warranted.

Here is the analytical mechanism worth naming directly. Substitution happens to careful people because the proxy question generates the same cognitive effort as the hard question. Forming an impression of a claimant's credibility requires attention, memory, and judgment, all the things we associate with analytical work. The feeling of working hard is identical whether you are answering the hard question or its proxy. That feeling cannot tell you which question you are answering. Only writing both questions down can.

Doug Lorch sustained high predictive accuracy across multiple years of the Good Judgment Project not because each individual forecast was brilliant but because the process that produced each forecast remained in contact with the actual question being asked. Regression to the mean eventually erodes most performance streaks; it did not erase Lorch's edge because the edge was not a lucky run. It was a method. One element of that method was checking whether the question being answered matched the question that needed answering before the answer was offered.

Rachel found that the restaurant group's loan application looked strong in the photographs and felt strong from the financials. She had been asking herself whether the group felt like a strong borrower. When she pulled the base rate for restaurant expansion loans of this size and vintage in this metro market, she found 22% default. Her debt-coverage calculation shifted. The proxy question had told her the answer she expected. The base rate told her something the proxy could not.

You cannot correct a substitution you have not named. The check is simple: write down the question you were asked, then write down the question you have actually been spending time on. If they are the same, proceed. If they differ, the work on the proxy may still be useful but it does not answer the target question, and presenting it as if it does is the last step in the substitution.

examples.title: David writes both questions side by side and finds his review only answers the easier one

planSpec.domain: pharmaceutical company safety committee reviewing a new drug's adverse event signal
planSpec.audience: a safety scientist who is the first reviewer of a flagged liver enzyme signal in a Phase III trial
planSpec.stakes: whether to pause the trial and report to regulators, or classify the signal as within expected range
planSpec.requiredBeat: the scientist realizes she has been answering a proxy rather than the target question; writing both questions side by side surfaces the substitution before the committee meets

examples.scenario:
Three liver enzyme charts are spread across the conference table, each with red circles around datapoints that flagged in the automated safety review. David photographs the charts, opens the signal review form, and begins writing.

The signal looks familiar. Three compounds in the same drug class have shown similar enzyme elevations at similar doses. The pattern is consistent with a class effect. He writes that in the review notes and feels confident the committee will align.

Before the meeting, he reads the review form question again: 'Describe the proposed causal mechanism linking this compound to the observed hepatic enzyme elevations in the study population.' He reads his notes: 'Pattern consistent with class effect from structurally similar compounds.'

He has not answered the question on the form. He has answered whether the pattern resembles a known class effect, which is a different and easier question. The form asks about mechanism. He has answered about resemblance. He writes both questions in the margin side by side. The gap is visible immediately. The trial pause question is still open. He must decide before the committee meets in two hours whether to submit the review as written with a note flagging the gap, or pull it and request the mechanistic data that would actually answer the form's question.
examples.whatToDo: Before any safety, legal, or regulatory review, write the exact target question on the top of the document, then read your analysis against it before submitting. When the analysis only addresses a proxy, mark it clearly and identify what additional evidence the target question requires.
examples.whyItMatters: In high-stakes review contexts, the substitution is particularly costly because it produces a confident answer that looks like it covers the hard question. Writing both questions explicitly makes the gap visible at the stage where it can still be addressed rather than at the stage where a decision has already been communicated.

examples.title: Kasia's debrief room has personality traits on the whiteboard where outcome metrics should be

planSpec.domain: corporate hiring committee evaluating a director-level candidate
planSpec.audience: a VP of People at a mid-size tech company running the final panel discussion on a senior hire
planSpec.stakes: a director role with four direct reports and a $400K budget
planSpec.requiredBeat: a panel member's resemblance comment triggers the VP's recognition that the committee has been answering a proxy rather than the target question

examples.scenario:
'She reminds me a lot of Damien,' the panel member says. 'Same energy. Same way of framing ambiguous problems.' Two other panelists nod.

Kasia is running the debrief. She has been in enough of these rooms to recognize what is happening: the committee is converging on resemblance to a known excellent performer as its primary signal. She looks at the whiteboard, where she has been recording the panel's observations: 'strategic thinker,' 'collaborative,' 'strong communicator.' Not a single outcome metric.

The target question for this hire is: based on verifiable outcome evidence, what is the probability this candidate performs at director level for the specific skills this role requires? The committee has been answering: does this person feel like someone we would recognize as excellent? The first question requires outcome data. The second question requires only pattern recognition from people who have worked with excellent performers.

Kasia pauses the debrief and asks each panelist to write down one verifiable outcome from the candidate's work history that speaks specifically to a skill the role requires. The exercise takes twelve minutes. Three of the panelists cannot write one down. Kasia must decide whether to halt the process and schedule a second structured reference call before any further deliberation, or allow the discussion to continue with the evidence the panel currently holds.
examples.whatToDo: Before finalizing any hiring decision, write the target question explicitly: 'What verifiable outcome evidence indicates this person will perform at [level] on [specific skill]?' Pause the process if the room cannot answer that question with evidence rather than impressions.
examples.whyItMatters: Resemblance to known excellent performers is a real signal but an imprecise proxy for the target question. The proxy converges the room quickly and feels rigorous because the people making the comparison are experienced. The gap between the proxy answer and the target answer only becomes visible when you write the target question and ask the room to answer it with evidence.

examples.title: Hugo's referral rate is six times the base rate, which tells him he has been answering the wrong question

planSpec.domain: insurance fraud investigation unit reviewing a property damage claim
planSpec.audience: a senior investigator deciding whether to refer a large water-damage claim to the special investigations unit
planSpec.stakes: a $280K claim and a referral decision that costs the company time and the claimant unnecessary scrutiny if wrong
planSpec.requiredBeat: the investigator's impression-based referral rate is six times the actual base rate, which reveals he has been answering a proxy rather than the target question

examples.scenario:
The manila folder is thick with claim photos and sticky notes. In the upper corner of the folder, Hugo's handwriting: 'Evasive on third call. Possible.' He has been keeping a running read on this claimant for two weeks.

His caseload review this quarter shows 18 referrals from 100 reviewed claims. He decides to check the base rate for water-damage claims of this size and geographic region: 3% documented fraud rate across comparable portfolios.

Three percent. He has been referring at 18%. Fifteen points above the base rate.

Hugo writes down the two questions. The question on the case file: is this claim fraudulent? The question he has been asking himself on each review: does this claimant seem like someone who would file a fraudulent claim? The base rate question and the impression question have been producing very different answers. He has been answering the impression question, writing it up as if it were the base rate question, and generating six times as many referrals as the actual fraud rate would warrant.

Hugo sets the current folder aside. He needs to decide: write the referral from the current impression, or run the base rate check first. He runs the check. The result changes the recommendation. He revises his process: every future referral now requires a documented base rate comparison before the impression goes in writing.
examples.whatToDo: Before any referral, escalation, or risk classification, record the base rate for the question you are trying to answer, then compare it to your current decision rate. A significant gap between the two is a signal that you have been answering a proxy question rather than the target one.
examples.whyItMatters: Impression-based screening feels rigorous because it requires attention and judgment. But impressions do not correct for the reference class, which is why impression-based rates consistently diverge from base rates when compared over a large enough sample. The base rate comparison is the only check that makes the substitution visible at scale.

examples.title: The menu looks strong and the base rate says 22% default, and those two facts do not resolve each other

planSpec.domain: credit analyst at a regional bank evaluating a small business loan application
planSpec.audience: a credit analyst reviewing a restaurant group's expansion loan request
planSpec.stakes: a $1.2M loan decision where the analyst's recommendation carries significant weight
planSpec.requiredBeat: the analyst notices she is answering a proxy question rather than the target; she looks up the base rate and finds it changes her debt-coverage calculation

examples.scenario:
You are a credit analyst reviewing a restaurant group's $1.2M expansion loan. Two monitors: the left one has the group's three-year financials, the right one has their website with interior photos and a menu that looks excellent. You find yourself using the phrase 'feels like a strong group' in your draft recommendation memo.

You pause. The question on the loan application is a probability question: what is the likelihood this borrower services and retires this loan according to the agreed schedule? The question you have been answering is: does this feel like a strong restaurant group?

You look up the default rate for restaurant expansion loans at this size and vintage in this metro market: 22%.

Twenty-two percent changes your debt-coverage calculation. Your original draft had used 8%, the same rate you applied to an established logistics company last week. The restaurant group has good photos and a coherent concept. It is also operating in a category with a structural default rate nearly three times your assumed rate. You must decide whether to revise the coverage ratio and rewrite the recommendation before it goes to the credit committee this afternoon, or flag the base rate finding in a footnote and let the committee weigh it. You choose to revise the recommendation entirely.
examples.whatToDo: Before writing any credit recommendation, look up the base rate for default or underperformance in the specific borrower category, loan size, and geography. Apply that base rate as your prior before adding any inside-view factors about the specific applicant.
examples.whyItMatters: A borrower who looks and feels like a strong candidate is giving you information about presentation, execution, and current momentum. The base rate gives you information about what happens to borrowers with that presentation and momentum in that category over time. Both inputs matter. Starting with the base rate prevents the inside view from displacing the reference class entirely.

examples.title: Lars runs a five-minute survey after writing both questions side by side and finds the answer is 6%

planSpec.domain: product manager at a software company deciding whether to build a feature based on two customer interviews
planSpec.audience: a PM who has just run two user research calls and is writing the feature brief
planSpec.stakes: six weeks of engineering time and a Q3 roadmap slot
planSpec.requiredBeat: writing both questions side by side reveals two proxies; a five-minute survey produces 6%, below threshold

examples.scenario:
How do you know when two enthusiastic customers are evidence rather than noise?

Lars has just run two user research calls for a proposed file-tagging feature. Both customers said they would use it constantly. He has written at the top of the feature brief: 'Customers love this.' The Q3 roadmap slot is open and six weeks of engineering capacity is available.

Before filing the brief, he writes down his actual target question: 'What proportion of users in the document-management segment of our 4,000-user base are meaningfully blocked by the problem this feature solves?' Then he writes down the questions he has actually been answering: 'Would I personally use this feature?' and 'Did these two customers sound enthusiastic about it?'

Both of the questions he answered are proxies. The first is about his own preferences, not the segment's. The second is about two customers who agreed to a research call, which is a self-selected group.

He sends a five-minute survey to a random sample of 200 users in the segment. The result: 6% report this as a meaningful blocker. His threshold for a six-week investment is 15%. The two calls were genuine and the customers were right about their own experience. The feature is the right answer to the problem. The problem affects 6% of the segment. Lars must decide whether to pull the feature from the Q3 roadmap now or bring the survey result to the planning meeting and let the team debate the threshold together.
examples.whatToDo: Before committing engineering time to a feature, write the target question explicitly: 'What proportion of the target segment is meaningfully blocked by this problem?' Then ask whether your current evidence answers that question or a proxy. If you only have qualitative calls, estimate the cost of getting a quantitative answer before making the investment decision.
examples.whyItMatters: Two enthusiastic customer calls is strong evidence that the problem is real for those customers. It is not evidence about segment prevalence, which is a different and harder question. Conflating the two is question substitution: the easy question (is the problem real?) is being presented as an answer to the harder one (is the problem prevalent enough to justify the investment?).

examples.title: Chloé cannot answer the reference-class question, which tells her everything about how she has been evaluating the source

planSpec.domain: investigative journalist evaluating whether to name a source on a document that contradicts official statements
planSpec.audience: a journalist deciding how much weight to give a source whose testimony aligns with what the journalist already suspects is true
planSpec.stakes: whether a story runs as presented or undergoes another month of verification
planSpec.requiredBeat: the journalist cannot answer the reference-class question, which tells her she has been relying on a proxy; this changes the publication timeline

examples.scenario:
At 3:15 in the afternoon, Chloé reads back through her interview transcript and the note she underlined twice: 'Credible. Genuine grievance.' She has been treating the source's account as a cornerstone of the story.

Before filing, she writes down two questions. The first is the question she has been answering: 'Does this source seem credible, and does she appear to have genuine motivation to tell the truth?' The second is the harder target question: 'How often have sources in comparable institutional positions who agreed with a reporter's prior hypothesis turned out to be accurate rather than motivated by grievance or self-interest?'

She cannot answer the second question. She does not have a reference class. She has not tracked how often sources who seemed credible and who confirmed her prior turned out to be substantially accurate over her career. The fact that she cannot answer the reference-class question tells her what she needs to know: she has been evaluating this source almost entirely on impression and alignment with her existing hypothesis.

She calls the story's editor and delays publication by three weeks while a second independent source is located. When the second source is found, their account differs from the first on two material details. The final story is narrower and more defensible.
examples.whatToDo: Before publishing any account that rests substantially on a single source, write down the reference-class question: 'How often have sources with this profile, in this institutional position, who agreed with my prior hypothesis, turned out to be accurate?' If you cannot answer it, treat the source's account as a hypothesis requiring independent corroboration rather than as confirmed.
examples.whyItMatters: A source who seems credible and confirms your prior is giving you evidence about their presentation and your expectations, not about the accuracy of the account. The reference-class question asks what happens to sources like this over time. If you cannot answer it, you are evaluating the proxy (does this seem credible?) without access to the base rate (how often does this profile produce accurate accounts?).

questions.prompt: A safety scientist reviewing a drug trial is asked to describe the causal mechanism linking a compound to observed liver enzyme elevations. After forty minutes of analysis, she writes that the pattern is 'consistent with a class effect from structurally similar compounds.' Her supervisor points out that she answered a different question than the one on the review form. What analytical error does this illustrate?
choices: Answering an easier proxy question rather than the harder target question, while presenting the result as if it addresses the target.
Replacing a probabilistic question with a simpler binary one in order to make the decision process faster and less cognitively demanding.
Substituting one expert's opinion or judgment for another's when the first expert's input is unavailable or insufficient.
questions.explanation: Question substitution is the specific cognitive pattern where a harder target question is replaced by an easier proxy that feels like it covers the target. The proxy generates real analytical work, which is why the substitution is invisible from the inside. The result is a confident answer to a question the decision actually required, presenting itself as if it addressed the harder question it replaced.

questions.prompt: A credit analyst writes 'feels like a strong borrower' in a loan recommendation memo and uses an 8% default assumption. When she checks the actual default rate for this loan category, she finds 22%. What analytical error does this reveal?
choices: She applied the correct inside-view judgment about borrower quality but failed to check the supporting financial documentation that would have revealed the warning signs.

She answered the proxy question ('does this borrower seem strong?') rather than the target question ('what is the probability of default for this category of borrower?'), which caused her to use the wrong reference class.
She overweighted the most recent quarterly results and underweighted the long-term base rate for this loan category, a standard availability bias error.
questions.explanation: The inside-view impression ('feels like a strong borrower') may be legitimate input, but it answered a proxy question rather than the target question, which requires a base rate estimate. The 14-percentage-point gap between her assumed rate and the actual category default rate is the cost of the substitution: the proxy question produced a number the target question would not support.

questions.prompt: A hiring committee uses 'she reminds me of our best people' as its primary evaluation criterion. What target question has it failed to answer?
choices: Whether the candidate has enough years of experience for the seniority level of the role.
Whether the candidate's communication style will fit with the team's working norms.
What the candidate's verifiable outcome record shows for the specific skills this role requires.
questions.explanation: Resemblance to excellent performers is a proxy for quality; it taps pattern recognition from experienced judges. The target question is whether verifiable past outcomes predict performance on the specific skills the role requires. The proxy and the target may correlate, but they are not the same: a candidate can strongly resemble a top performer without having the outcome record that would justify that resemblance as a prediction.

questions.prompt: Robert Jervis's analysis of the Iraq WMD intelligence failure argues that different confidence levels could have changed the political pathway. What does this reveal about the cost of question substitution at scale?
choices: That intelligence agencies should defer to political leaders on questions of national security rather than issue independent probability assessments.
That substituting an easier behavioral question for a harder evidentiary question produced overconfident conclusions that foreclosed options that lower stated confidence might have preserved.
That intelligence failure is primarily the result of insufficient data, not analytical method, and that more data would have prevented the error.
questions.explanation: Jervis's point is that expressing 70% instead of 95% would have been honest given the actual evidentiary basis, and that confidence levels at scale affect policy decisions. The behavioral proxy (does he act like someone concealing weapons?) was overconfident as an answer to the evidentiary target (does he have weapons?). Stating the real uncertainty level at that scale would have moved policy, which is what the substitution cost.

questions.prompt: Hugo, a senior insurance investigator, has been referring claims for fraud investigation at a rate of 18%, yet the documented fraud rate for his claim type is only 3%. When he reviews his process, he realizes he has been carefully evaluating each claimant's demeanor, history, and behavior. Why does this careful work fail to detect that he has been answering the wrong question?
choices: Because the proxy question generates the same subjective feeling of analytical effort as the hard question, making the substitution invisible without an external check.
Because most analysts lack training in reference class forecasting and do not know how to formulate the target question correctly.
Because organizations reward confident answers regardless of whether they address the right question, creating incentives to substitute.
questions.explanation: The subjective experience of forming an impression, running a comparison, or pattern-matching is indistinguishable from the experience of answering the harder target question. The work feels equally demanding in both cases. An experienced analyst forming a credibility impression of a source is doing real analytical work; the result just addresses a different question than the one that needs answering. Writing both questions down is the only check that makes the substitution visible.

questions.prompt: A product manager runs two customer interviews and both respond enthusiastically to a proposed feature. She treats this as strong evidence that the feature should be built. What question has she failed to answer?
choices: Whether the feature's implementation cost is proportionate to the expected revenue impact.
Whether the two customers' technical requirements are compatible with the current platform architecture.
What proportion of the full target user segment is meaningfully blocked by the problem the feature addresses.
questions.explanation: Two enthusiastic interviews confirm that the problem is real for those customers. They do not answer the segment prevalence question, which is what investment decisions require. The proxy questions ('do I find this useful?' and 'did these customers respond positively?') produce real signal about problem validity; they do not produce signal about how many users are affected, which is the variable that determines whether the investment is proportionate.

questions.prompt: Doug Lorch sustained high predictive accuracy across multiple years of the Good Judgment Project without regression to the mean erasing his edge. What does this suggest about the relationship between sustained accuracy and question discipline?
choices: That superior access to private or proprietary information, rather than analytical method or discipline, is the primary source of any durable forecasting advantage.

That sustained accuracy over many predictions is evidence of a method that consistently addresses the target question rather than a proxy, because luck alone regresses to average across a large prediction set.
That forecasting tournaments produce artificially stable accuracy results because participants systematically self-select for demonstrated performance consistency over time.
questions.explanation: Regression to the mean predicts that lucky performance streaks decay toward average over large samples. Sustained accuracy across many predictions and multiple years is not well explained by luck alone. A method that consistently addresses the actual question being scored, rather than a substitute that happens to correlate with the answer, is a more parsimonious explanation for performance that outlasts a streak.

questions.prompt: An investigative journalist discovers she cannot answer the reference-class question for her primary source: 'How often have sources in this institutional position who confirmed my prior turned out to be accurate?' What should she do with this finding?
choices: Treat the source as a hypothesis requiring independent corroboration rather than as confirmed evidence, and build verification into the publication timeline.
Replace impression-based evaluation with a standardized credibility checklist before any source is quoted.
Suspend use of anonymous sources entirely until reference-class data on source accuracy is available from published research.
questions.explanation: Not being able to answer the reference-class question reveals that source evaluation has been based entirely on proxy signals (impression, apparent motivation, alignment with prior). The appropriate response is not to build a checklist or abandon anonymous sources but to treat the account as a hypothesis rather than a confirmed fact, and to build independent corroboration into the process before publication.

questions.prompt: A manager argues that proxy questions are acceptable shortcuts when the hard question is genuinely unanswerable with available data, and that demanding the target question in all cases leads to paralysis. Is this argument valid?
choices: Yes, because proxy questions are genuinely the most rigorous analytical tool available when the target question lacks sufficient supporting data.

Partly valid for the premise, but the conclusion does not follow: acknowledging a proxy as a proxy (and marking confidence accordingly) is different from presenting a proxy answer as if it addressed the target.
No, because the inability to answer the hard question directly is always a clear signal that more thorough data collection is required before any meaningful decision is made.
questions.explanation: The manager's observation that some target questions are genuinely hard to answer directly is correct. The error is in the conclusion. Using a proxy is sometimes unavoidable; presenting the proxy answer at target-question confidence is the substitution error. A forensic investigator who cannot know for certain whether fraud occurred can still note that her impression-based assessment is a proxy, mark the uncertainty accordingly, and avoid presenting an 18% referral rate as if it were grounded in a 3% base rate.

reviewCards.front: What is question substitution, and why is it invisible from the inside?
reviewCards.back: Question substitution is replacing the target question with an easier proxy while presenting the result as if it addresses the target. It is invisible because the proxy generates the same subjective feeling of analytical effort as the hard question. The work feels like the real work regardless of which question it actually answers.

reviewCards.front: What was the substitution in the Iraq WMD intelligence case, and what did Jervis argue should have been different?
reviewCards.back: The target question was whether Hussein actually had weapons. The question that got answered was whether his behavior resembled someone concealing weapons. Jervis argued that expressing 70% instead of 95% would have been honest to the actual evidentiary basis, and that honesty at that confidence level changes policy outcomes.

reviewCards.front: What is the practical check for detecting whether you have substituted a proxy for the target question?
reviewCards.back: Write down the exact question you were asked. Then write down the question you have actually been spending time on. If they differ, you have substituted. The work on the proxy may still be useful, but it does not answer the target question and should not be presented as if it does.

reviewCards.front: Why does a large divergence between impression-based rates and base rates signal question substitution?
reviewCards.back: If a decision-maker's impression-based referral or classification rate consistently diverges from the base rate for the question being decided, the decision-maker has been answering a proxy (does this case seem like X?) rather than the target (what rate of cases in this category are actually X?). The gap is the accumulated cost of the substitution across many decisions.

reviewCards.front: How does sustained accuracy in the Good Judgment Project bear on the skill-versus-luck question?
reviewCards.back: Luck-based performance streaks regress to average over large prediction sets because luck is random. Sustained accuracy across many predictions and multiple years is better explained by a method that consistently addresses the actual question being scored. Doug Lorch's sustained edge suggests a process that stays on the real question rather than a lucky run on proxies.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Before doing analytical work on any significant decision, write the target question explicitly in one sentence. After completing the analysis, check whether your conclusion answers that sentence or a different one. If they do not match, mark the confidence level to reflect the proxy rather than the target.

ifThenPlans.context: Before writing a recommendation, brief, or assessment
ifThenPlans.plan: If you find yourself generating a confident conclusion before you have written down the exact target question you were asked to answer, then write the target question first, read your draft against it, and identify whether your conclusion addresses it or a proxy.

ifThenPlans.context: When a base rate is available for the question you are answering
ifThenPlans.plan: If your impression-based assessment differs significantly from the base rate for this case category, then treat the base rate as your prior and name the inside-view factors that move your estimate from the base rate rather than replacing the base rate with the impression.

ifThenPlans.context: In any group decision-making process where impressions or resemblance are being cited as evidence
ifThenPlans.plan: If the room is converging on 'seems like' or 'reminds me of' language, then ask what verifiable outcome evidence the convergence rests on and request that one such piece of evidence be named before the discussion closes.

ifThenPlans.context: After a decision has been made and the outcome is known
ifThenPlans.plan: If the outcome differed from your prediction, review whether you answered the target question or a proxy. If you answered a proxy, note what the target question actually required and what evidence would have been needed to answer it directly.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Find one ongoing analysis or decision where you have a working conclusion. Write down the exact question you were supposed to answer. Then write down the question your conclusion actually answers. If they are different, note the gap and identify one piece of evidence that would address the target question rather than the proxy.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, review one decision you made where you had high confidence in your conclusion. Write down both the target question and the question you actually answered. Over several months, a pattern of which types of questions you tend to substitute will become visible and correctable.

memorableLines.text: The substituted question is not the wrong question. It is the question that arrived first, felt like the right one, and got answered while the right one waited.
memorableLines.why: It reframes substitution as timing and arrival sequence rather than incompetence, which is what makes it accurate and worth keeping.

memorableLines.text: The question on paper was whether he had the weapons. The question that actually got answered was whether he was acting like someone who did.
memorableLines.why: It names the Iraq WMD substitution with the precision of a before-and-after comparison, making the gap between target and proxy concrete rather than abstract.

memorableLines.text: You cannot correct a substitution you have not named.
memorableLines.why: Eleven words that make the entire argument actionable: the solution to question substitution is naming it, not avoiding hard questions.

chapters.title: Supersmart?
chapters.hook: Enrico Fermi did not know how many piano tuners worked in Chicago. He built the number from smaller numbers he could estimate separately, and his answer was usually within a factor of two. That is not genius. That is method.
chapters.counterintuition: Breaking a big uncertain question into smaller uncertain parts feels like multiplying the uncertainty. It does not. Independent estimation errors partially cancel each other, and naming each component forces you to confront assumptions you would otherwise leave invisible.
chapters.tryThisNow: Find one number you need to estimate this week: a project cost, a timeline, an audience size, a conversion rate. Before guessing, write three components the total is made of. Look up or estimate each component separately. Multiply or add them. Compare that number to your gut estimate. The gap between them is what decomposition is for.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Raw intelligence without a method produces brilliant-sounding wrong answers. Decompose the question into estimable parts, anchor each on the reference class, then adjust for what you know specifically.

breakdown.fastRead:
Frida had a gut number for the surgery: three hours. She had done similar revisions many times. But this case had an unusual hardware configuration on the CT scan that her gut had not accounted for.

She broke it down instead. Standard revision time from her last 12 cases: two and a half hours. Additional time for this specific complication pattern: forty minutes. Hardware removal estimate: thirty minutes. Buffer for unexpected findings: fifteen minutes. Total: four hours and five minutes.

The decomposition is not a substitute for knowing things. It is a structure for not knowing things in a disciplined way.

The gut estimate was off by more than an hour. Not because Frida's judgment was poor, but because the gut estimate had no components to adjust on their own. The decomposition did. When the hardware estimate changed, only one component changed with it.
breakdown.deepRead:
Enrico Fermi did not guess at the number of piano tuners in Chicago. He built the number from smaller guesses that could each be checked separately.

How many households in Chicago? Around 1.5 million. What fraction own a piano? About one in twenty. How often does a piano need tuning? About once a year. How long does a tuning take, with travel? About two hours. How many working hours does a tuner have in a year? About 2,000. Divide: 1.5 million times 0.05 gives 75,000 pianos. Each requires two hours once a year, so 150,000 hours of demand. Divided by 2,000 hours per tuner: 75 piano tuners. The actual number, when checked, was close.

The components were uncertain. But they were uncertain in different directions. An overestimate on piano ownership ran against an underestimate on tuning frequency. Independent errors partially cancel. A single gut guess has no such correction mechanism.

When Bill Flack looked at the Arafat polonium story (Bill Flack's Arafat polonium case, as it was catalogued in the GJP data), he started somewhere else. The inside-view narrative was compelling: sophisticated actor, state-level capability, politically motivated elimination. Flack went to the outside view first. How often do leaders in comparable political circumstances die by poisoning versus other causes? What is the fraction of high-profile deaths attributed to foul play that are later confirmed as such? The reference class was considerably more skeptical than the headlines implied.

Flack's probability came in lower than the narrative suggested. Not because the polonium story was definitely wrong, but because the reference class for 'compelling assassination narrative' does not confirm at the rate that compelling narratives imply. That is the discipline: reference class first, narrative second. Consulting specific knowledge before the reference class almost always inflates confidence past what the evidence warrants.
breakdown.fullRead:
Michael's board deck had 'TAM: $2.8B' on slide four. He had found a market research report that felt right and used its top-level number. The board's first question would be: how did you get to that number?

He went back to the whiteboard. Target companies in the sector: roughly 6,000 from public databases. Fraction facing the specific regulatory pressure: 30% from industry association data. Fraction currently using any software to manage it: 12% from an analyst estimate. Willingness to pay at his price point: $18,000 per year from three customer interviews. Product: 6,000 times 0.30 times 0.12 times $18,000 equals roughly $3.9 million in reachable annual contract value. His gut number was $2.8 billion. The decomposed number was $3.9 million.

The 40% adjustment that matters is not from $2.8B to something lower. It is from whatever your gut number is to whatever the decomposition says. Michael's decomposed number was defensible. He used it in the deck with the four components shown.

Aman found four analogous cycling infrastructure projects in comparable cities. The cost-per-kilometer numbers ranged from $380K to $470K across the reference class, giving him a midpoint near $425K before examining local conditions. He had the reference class number before he looked at the local project specs.

The outside view feels like giving up. That feeling is a signal it is working. When you consult the reference class before examining your specific case in detail, the move clears away everything that makes your case feel personal and specific. The reference class number looks like it could have come from anywhere. That abstraction is the point: if the number felt specific before you adjusted for local factors, it would already have been contaminated by inside-view reasoning before the reference class could correct it.

Aman then found one local distinguishing factor: union labor rates in his city ran 22% above the reference class average. He adjusted the estimate from $425K per kilometer to $515K. His director had already communicated $410K to the council committee. The conversation before the meeting was uncomfortable. It was also necessary. An estimate that has not been stress-tested against a reference class is only an inside-view number wearing the look of an estimate.

Sophie built the conference attendance estimate from components. Total registrants in the client's industry association email list: 12,000. Historical open rate for comparable conference invitations: 28%. Conversion from open to registration: 18%. Expected no-show rate from three analogous events: 22%. The product was roughly 340 attendees. The client had expected 500. Sophie presented 340 with confidence intervals and the rationale behind each component. The client reset their expectations before the venue deposit was paid.

Jonas ran the same sequence in a different domain. The question was not attendance but medication buffer: would current supply cover a six-week rural health surge? He decomposed: current census (85 patients), surge multiplier from two years of seasonal data (1.4x), average daily doses per patient for the three highest-demand medications, and days of supply on hand. The answer was 11 days of buffer under surge conditions, below the safe threshold. The emergency order was placed before the surge rather than during it.

Decomposition works even when every component is imprecise. Each component's error is independent of the others', which means they partially cancel. The gut estimate has no such cancellation; its errors flow from a single judgment that can be confidently wrong in one direction by any amount.

examples.title: Michael's TAM decomposition comes back 40% below his gut number, and he uses it anyway

planSpec.domain: startup founder estimating addressable market for a niche B2B compliance software product
planSpec.audience: a founder preparing a board deck whose market size claim is currently a guess
planSpec.stakes: Series A term sheet discussion where the investor's first question will be 'how did you get to that number?'
planSpec.requiredBeat: the four-component decomposition returns 40% below the gut estimate; the founder uses the defensible number rather than the comfortable one

examples.scenario:
'How did you get to that number?' the Series A lead asks, pointing at slide four. 'That's a big market for a pretty specific compliance use case.'

Michael has been dreading this question since he built the slide. He found a large market research report and used its top-level figure. He knows the board will push.

That evening, he goes back to the whiteboard. Four components: the total number of companies in the target sector (roughly 6,000, from two public databases); the fraction facing the specific regulatory pressure that drives demand for his product (30%, from industry association data); the fraction currently using any software to manage this problem (12%, from an analyst estimate); and the willingness-to-pay range at his price point ($18,000 per year, from three customer interviews). Multiply: 6,000 times 0.30 times 0.12 gives 216 companies. Times $18,000 gives $3.9M in reachable annual contract value.

His original slide said $2.8B. The decomposed estimate is $3.9M in near-term reachable value. He rewrites the slide. The new version shows all four components and their sources. In the next board meeting, the Series A lead calls it the most defensible TAM analysis she has seen from an early-stage company.
examples.whatToDo: Before committing a market size estimate to a board deck or investor meeting, decompose it into three or four components that can each be independently sourced. The decomposed number may be lower than your gut estimate. Use it: a defensible lower number is worth more in a term sheet conversation than an indefensible higher one.
examples.whyItMatters: A market size from a single report number has no components an investor can challenge or refine. A decomposed estimate turns the question from 'do you believe this number?' into 'which of these components do you read differently?' That is a conversation the founder can have. The gut number closes that conversation before it opens.

examples.title: Frida's decomposed estimate runs 25 minutes long and changes the afternoon schedule

planSpec.domain: orthopedic surgeon estimating operative time for a complex revision hip replacement she has not done in this exact configuration before
planSpec.audience: a surgeon scheduling a surgery list whose time estimate determines whether a second case can be added to the afternoon
